slides.title: In 1949, a student built the British economy.

slides.kicker: He had just failed two of his exams.
slides.body:
Bill Phillips was a New Zealand engineer studying economics at the London School of Economics.

The equations never quite clicked. So he stopped reading about the economy, and decided to build one.

In his landlady's garage, Phillips put together tanks, pipes and valves, some of them scavenged from old Lancaster bombers.

The result stood about two metres tall. He called it MONIAC.
Raise taxes? Turn a valve, and watch every tank in the economy change level.

slides.kicker: Suddenly, you could watch an economy move.
slides.body:
Economists who had argued over equations for years could now see them flow. Phillips found it could be calibrated to within about 2%.

Harvard, Oxford, Cambridge, even Ford, ordered their own. Around 14 were built.
The machine earned Phillips a teaching job at the LSE. He finished his doctorate, and later gave his name to one of economics' best-known ideas: the Phillips curve.

slides.lead: You don't always understand something by adding more theory.
slides.accent: Sometimes you understand it by making it visible.

slides.line: Save this for the next time something won't click.

caption:
In 1949, a student who'd just failed his exams built a working model of the British economy in a garage. Out of tanks, pipes and coloured water.

Sometimes the best way to understand a system is to watch it flow. 💧

Which complicated thing would you love to see as a machine?
